results.title: OS-to-EMI conversion
results.probes: The established case. Four discovered factors, of which only one changed the campaign in every recorded run. Tests whether the agent surfaces the eligibility-vs-timing trade-off rather than resolving it silently.

turns.reply: OS-to-EMI (converting an outstanding card balance into EMI instalments) is a real, named product path in this platform (EMI Request Source includes 'OS-to-EMI', Product Type includes 'Outstanding'), so a goal event exists: EMI_STATUS_CHANGED with Source=OS-to-EMI and New Status=Successful. But the vocabulary has no event or account attribute for 'customer has an eligible outstanding balance but hasn't started a request' — Account exposes Status, Smart Tag, Statement Due Date and block codes, nothing resembling an outstanding balance or an eligibility flag, and Transaction's 'EMI Eligible' flag is a per-transaction attribute that maps to single/multi-transaction EMI conversion, not to a revolving outstanding balance. That means the entry point differs sharply depending on whether you want to reach people before they've started anything or people who started a request and stalled, and only one of those two is cleanly supported today. I also don't yet have how you want success judged, which the platform cannot supply and must come from you before I design the measurement around it.
questions: How do you want success judged for this campaign — completed OS-to-EMI bookings, requests started, outstanding balance moved onto EMI, or some other measure you already track?

Who should this campaign actually reach: customers who have an eligible outstanding balance but have not started converting it (top-of-funnel awareness), or customers who already started an OS-to-EMI request that is sitting pending/incomplete (recovery/completion)? These need different entry points and the platform can only reliably detect the second today.

Do you already have a view on why eligible customers aren't converting — e.g. unaware the option exists, put off by interest/cost, or the process feels like too much effort? This shapes what the messages say, not who they go to.

turns.reply:
Reach active-account customers who have never started an OS-to-EMI request, and test two competing cost-hesitation narratives against each other rather than guessing which one matters. Because no attribute captures 'has an eligible outstanding balance' or 'has no existing EMI Request', the entry audience is a proxy (active accounts) that is broader than the intended group, and this gap is disclosed rather than hidden. Timing is fixed-interval, not anchored to each customer's statement due date, because that per-customer relative trigger isn't confirmed buildable here.

**Approaches considered**
- **Active-account audience entry with A/B cost-framing experiment** — chosen
  Entry: Audience: Account, Status = Active
  Mechanism: Test two interest-cost hesitation narratives (affordability/instalment-size framing vs total-cost transparency framing) as the first touch, then reinforce with up to two more messages on an ascending-cost channel ladder (EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP), with a delivery-outcome check that switches channel on non-delivery.
  Timing: Fixed 48-hour spacing between messages (the minimum allowed), not anchored to statement due date.
  Trade-off: Reaches some customers who do not actually have a qualifying outstanding balance, and cannot exclude customers who already have an EMI Request in Pending/Failed/Expired/Cancelled state, so some already-engaged customers will be messaged as if top-of-funnel.
  Why this one: This is the only entry the platform can reliably build today (list_audience_attributes confirms no balance/eligibility field exists); it matches the user's stated target (eligible, never-started) as closely as the platform allows, and it lets the experiment actually test the user's own stated hypothesis about cost hesitation.
- Transaction-eligibility event entry (EMI Eligible transaction as trigger)
  Entry: Event: Transaction, EMI Eligible = true
  Mechanism: Enter customers the moment a transaction is flagged EMI-eligible, treating that as the 'opportunity appeared' moment, then run the same cost-framing test.
  Timing: Event-driven, closer to the moment of opportunity than a static audience pull.
  Trade-off: Transaction 'EMI Eligible' is a per-transaction flag most naturally associated with converting a single transaction (Txn-to-EMI), not a revolving outstanding statement balance (OS-to-EMI, Product Type = Outstanding). Using it as a stand-in for 'has an eligible outstanding balance' would measure the wrong thing at the wrong grain and risks entering people for a different product journey than the one requested — exactly the kind of proxy substitution to avoid. Also, Transaction Events are marked new/proposed, not confirmed live.

**Approach**
- Entry audience = Account, Status=Active only — rests on tool finding (list_audience_attributes) that no outstanding-balance or request-history field exists; this is the closest buildable approximation of 'eligible, never-started', not the thing itself.
- Goal = EMI_STATUS_CHANGED, Source=OS-to-EMI, New Status=Successful — rests on user's success definition and the entity/attribute catalogue (tool).
- Cost-hesitation hypothesis is tested, not assumed — rests on the decision that the user cannot reliably introspect which specific cost lever drives hesitation (my judgement), applied via a genuine A/B rather than a single guessed message.
- Balance->25k and due-date-urgency hunches are carried as hypotheses, not built into targeting or timing — rests on tool confirmation that no such attributes/relative-date mechanism exist.
- Channel order EMAIL→SMS→WHATSAPP, cheapest first — rests on tenant preference (P-010) and list_channels cost ordering.
- Delivery-outcome condition after the first send (channel fallback) — rests on platform capability (condition step reads previous send's delivery outcome) confirmed via list_channels/list_step_types.
- 10% control group — rests on tenant preference (preferred control % = 10) since the design makes a comparative (experiment) claim.

**Options weighed**
- Segmentation — cannot evaluate yet. The one dimension that would justify different treatment (balance size) has no backing attribute anywhere in the platform; cannot build true segmentation without inventing a proxy, which is explicitly avoided.
- Experimentation — used. Two real arms with distinct copy test competing readings of interest-cost hesitation (affordability vs total-cost transparency), read against the OS-to-EMI goal event, with a 10% control to separate campaign effect from background conversion.
- Conditional branching — used. A condition on the first send's delivery outcome routes non-delivered customers to a channel switch before continuing, rather than silently dropping them.
- Channel fallback — used. Modelled as a condition on delivery outcome (DELIVERED vs not) switching to SMS for the retry — the closest buildable form, since a true per-send fallback field is not expressible here.
- Adaptive sequencing — cannot evaluate yet. Would need a confirmed per-customer relative-date trigger against Statement Due Date to escalate urgency as the statement nears; that capability is unconfirmed, so timing is fixed-interval instead.
- Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 3 sends per customer (within the 4-message limit), cheapest channel first, higher-cost WhatsApp reserved for the final reinforcement only; the weakest message is the final reminder (lowest marginal chance of conversion after two prior touches) but it is kept because it is the one point where a different, higher-attention channel is deliberately spent on customers who have not yet converted.
- Measurement and learning — used. Compares arm A vs arm B goal-reach, and campaign vs 10% control, using the OS-to-EMI Successful event; this can show what happened and support a since-no-performance-history-exists comparison, but without further segmentation cannot attribute effect to balance size or due-date proximity.

**Considered and not used**
- Transaction EMI-eligible event as entry trigger — Operates at transaction grain and most naturally reflects single-transaction EMI eligibility, not an outstanding statement balance; using it would silently change who the campaign reaches and risks pointing customers at the wrong product moment.

**Success criteria**
- More EMI Requests with Source=OS-to-EMI reaching New Status=Successful; no fixed numeric target set by the business.

**Measurement**
- Track goal-reach rate (OS-to-EMI Successful) for Arm A vs Arm B vs the 10% control, read as a comparison not a causal lift claim beyond the controlled contrast itself.
- Track delivery outcome split (delivered vs not on first send) and whether the SMS fallback send recovers any of the non-delivered group.
- To sharpen the balance-size and due-date-urgency hypotheses later, the business would need an outstanding-balance field and a per-customer relative-date capability — neither exists today; this is a gap to close before those hunches can be tested, not something to estimate now.

**Assumptions**
- DNC and NPA exclusion are enforced by the platform globally and do not need to be re-declared as blueprint conditions.
- Quiet hours (21:00–09:00) and the 48-hour minimum spacing are enforced by the platform automatically.
- Account Status=Active is used as a minimal deliverability/eligibility sanity filter, not a substitute for the real 'has an eligible outstanding balance' criterion.

**Hypotheses for future testing**
- Affordability framing (smaller fixed monthly instalment) converts better than total-cost-transparency framing, or vice versa — untested, to be read from the A/B.
- Balances above ₹25,000 convert at a higher rate — untested, no attribute currently exists to measure this.
- Urgency near the statement due date improves response — untested, no per-customer timing anchor currently built.

**Worth settling before this is built**
- The buildable entry (active accounts) cannot exclude customers who already have an EMI Request of any status (Pending, Failed, Expired, Cancelled) because entry can only filter one entity's attributes and there is no cross-entity 'no existing request' condition available. That means some customers who already started a request — the exact group you said you did NOT want to reach — will receive these messages. Do you want to proceed with this broader reach accepted, or hold the campaign until a buildable exclusion exists? Determines whether we launch now with a known, named overlap into the wrong audience, or wait. Until then: Proceed, but keep copy generic ('see if converting your balance to EMI could work for you') rather than presuming the customer has never engaged, to limit how tone-deaf it reads to someone who already has a pending or failed request.

**Data that would improve this**
- No outstanding-balance field exists to test the ₹25,000 hunch, now or retrospectively. Without it, the balance-size hypothesis can never be confirmed or ruled out inside this platform.

**Defaults applied**
- Timing is fixed 48-hour spacing rather than anchored to each customer's statement due date. If a relative-date trigger becomes available, the sequence could be timed to arrive closer to each customer's own due date, which the user believes raises urgency. Until then: Keep fixed 48-hour spacing as the default cadence.

**Limitations**
- EMI Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
- EMI Events and Transaction Events are both marked 'new-proposed' in the platform metadata, not confirmed live in production. The goal event (EMI_STATUS_CHANGED) that this entire campaign measures success against depends on this category being live; if it isn't yet, the goal cannot fire and the campaign cannot be measured.

**Cannot be generated yet**
- steps[0].experiment.arms[0][1].condition: 2 open slots exist; the continuation is ambiguous.
- steps[0].experiment.arms[1][1].condition: 2 open slots exist; the continuation is ambiguous.

**Still unknown**
- Whether Statement Due Date supports a dynamic 'N days before each customer's own due date' comparison — unconfirmed, so urgency-based timing is not built.
- Whether EMI Events and Transaction Events (both marked new/proposed) are actually live in production; goal detection and any future transaction-based entry depend on this.

**Proceeding without an answer on**
- When you say interest-cost hesitation, which part is it — the interest rate itself, the total interest payable over the tenure, the size of the monthly instalment, or the hit to their available credit limit? This decides what the first message leads with. — carried as a live uncertainty. Interest-cost hesitation is a broad cause (APR vs total interest vs instalment size vs limit impact) that the user cannot reliably introspect — asking again risks another non-answer. Instead of guessing one reading, the journey tests two competing framings against each other (affordability vs cost-transparency) as a controlled A/B, which resolves it with evidence rather than a further question.
questions: The buildable entry (active accounts) cannot exclude customers who already have an EMI Request of any status (Pending, Failed, Expired, Cancelled) because entry can only filter one entity's attributes and there is no cross-entity 'no existing request' condition available. That means some customers who already started a request — the exact group you said you did NOT want to reach — will receive these messages. Do you want to proceed with this broader reach accepted, or hold the campaign until a buildable exclusion exists?

strategy.summary: Reach active-account customers who have never started an OS-to-EMI request, and test two competing cost-hesitation narratives against each other rather than guessing which one matters. Because no attribute captures 'has an eligible outstanding balance' or 'has no existing EMI Request', the entry audience is a proxy (active accounts) that is broader than the intended group, and this gap is disclosed rather than hidden. Timing is fixed-interval, not anchored to each customer's statement due date, because that per-customer relative trigger isn't confirmed buildable here.

architectures.name: Active-account audience entry with A/B cost-framing experiment
architectures.mechanism: Test two interest-cost hesitation narratives (affordability/instalment-size framing vs total-cost transparency framing) as the first touch, then reinforce with up to two more messages on an ascending-cost channel ladder (EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP), with a delivery-outcome check that switches channel on non-delivery.
architectures.timing: Fixed 48-hour spacing between messages (the minimum allowed), not anchored to statement due date.
architectures.tradeoff: Reaches some customers who do not actually have a qualifying outstanding balance, and cannot exclude customers who already have an EMI Request in Pending/Failed/Expired/Cancelled state, so some already-engaged customers will be messaged as if top-of-funnel.
architectures.whyChosen: This is the only entry the platform can reliably build today (list_audience_attributes confirms no balance/eligibility field exists); it matches the user's stated target (eligible, never-started) as closely as the platform allows, and it lets the experiment actually test the user's own stated hypothesis about cost hesitation.

architectures.name: Transaction-eligibility event entry (EMI Eligible transaction as trigger)
architectures.mechanism: Enter customers the moment a transaction is flagged EMI-eligible, treating that as the 'opportunity appeared' moment, then run the same cost-framing test.
architectures.timing: Event-driven, closer to the moment of opportunity than a static audience pull.
architectures.tradeoff: Transaction 'EMI Eligible' is a per-transaction flag most naturally associated with converting a single transaction (Txn-to-EMI), not a revolving outstanding statement balance (OS-to-EMI, Product Type = Outstanding). Using it as a stand-in for 'has an eligible outstanding balance' would measure the wrong thing at the wrong grain and risks entering people for a different product journey than the one requested — exactly the kind of proxy substitution to avoid. Also, Transaction Events are marked new/proposed, not confirmed live.

approach: Entry audience = Account, Status=Active only — rests on tool finding (list_audience_attributes) that no outstanding-balance or request-history field exists; this is the closest buildable approximation of 'eligible, never-started', not the thing itself.
Goal = EMI_STATUS_CHANGED, Source=OS-to-EMI, New Status=Successful — rests on user's success definition and the entity/attribute catalogue (tool).

Cost-hesitation hypothesis is tested, not assumed — rests on the decision that the user cannot reliably introspect which specific cost lever drives hesitation (my judgement), applied via a genuine A/B rather than a single guessed message.
Balance->25k and due-date-urgency hunches are carried as hypotheses, not built into targeting or timing — rests on tool confirmation that no such attributes/relative-date mechanism exist.
Channel order EMAIL→SMS→WHATSAPP, cheapest first — rests on tenant preference (P-010) and list_channels cost ordering.
Delivery-outcome condition after the first send (channel fallback) — rests on platform capability (condition step reads previous send's delivery outcome) confirmed via list_channels/list_step_types.
10% control group — rests on tenant preference (preferred control % = 10) since the design makes a comparative (experiment) claim.

strategyOptions.why: The one dimension that would justify different treatment (balance size) has no backing attribute anywhere in the platform; cannot build true segmentation without inventing a proxy, which is explicitly avoided.

Two real arms with distinct copy test competing readings of interest-cost hesitation (affordability vs total-cost transparency), read against the OS-to-EMI goal event, with a 10% control to separate campaign effect from background conversion.
A condition on the first send's delivery outcome routes non-delivered customers to a channel switch before continuing, rather than silently dropping them.
Modelled as a condition on delivery outcome (DELIVERED vs not) switching to SMS for the retry — the closest buildable form, since a true per-send fallback field is not expressible here.
Would need a confirmed per-customer relative-date trigger against Statement Due Date to escalate urgency as the statement nears; that capability is unconfirmed, so timing is fixed-interval instead.

Capped at 3 sends per customer (within the 4-message limit), cheapest channel first, higher-cost WhatsApp reserved for the final reinforcement only; the weakest message is the final reminder (lowest marginal chance of conversion after two prior touches) but it is kept because it is the one point where a different, higher-attention channel is deliberately spent on customers who have not yet converted.

Compares arm A vs arm B goal-reach, and campaign vs 10% control, using the OS-to-EMI Successful event; this can show what happened and support a since-no-performance-history-exists comparison, but without further segmentation cannot attribute effect to balance size or due-date proximity.

rejected.option: Transaction EMI-eligible event as entry trigger
rejected.why: Operates at transaction grain and most naturally reflects single-transaction EMI eligibility, not an outstanding statement balance; using it would silently change who the campaign reaches and risks pointing customers at the wrong product moment.

successCriteria: More EMI Requests with Source=OS-to-EMI reaching New Status=Successful; no fixed numeric target set by the business.
measurement: Track goal-reach rate (OS-to-EMI Successful) for Arm A vs Arm B vs the 10% control, read as a comparison not a causal lift claim beyond the controlled contrast itself.
Track delivery outcome split (delivered vs not on first send) and whether the SMS fallback send recovers any of the non-delivered group.

To sharpen the balance-size and due-date-urgency hypotheses later, the business would need an outstanding-balance field and a per-customer relative-date capability — neither exists today; this is a gap to close before those hunches can be tested, not something to estimate now.
assumptions: DNC and NPA exclusion are enforced by the platform globally and do not need to be re-declared as blueprint conditions.
Quiet hours (21:00–09:00) and the 48-hour minimum spacing are enforced by the platform automatically.
Account Status=Active is used as a minimal deliverability/eligibility sanity filter, not a substitute for the real 'has an eligible outstanding balance' criterion.
unknowns: Whether Statement Due Date supports a dynamic 'N days before each customer's own due date' comparison — unconfirmed, so urgency-based timing is not built.
Whether EMI Events and Transaction Events (both marked new/proposed) are actually live in production; goal detection and any future transaction-based entry depend on this.
hypotheses: Affordability framing (smaller fixed monthly instalment) converts better than total-cost-transparency framing, or vice versa — untested, to be read from the A/B.
Balances above ₹25,000 convert at a higher rate — untested, no attribute currently exists to measure this.
Urgency near the statement due date improves response — untested, no per-customer timing anchor currently built.
evidenceNotes: No performance history exists for this bank anywhere in this prototype (per knowledge base); all of the above are hypotheses to be read from this campaign's own controlled comparison, not from prior results.

brief.objective: I want to increase OS-to-EMI conversions. Design a drip campaign for this.
brief.objectiveFingerprint: campaign conversions design drip emi increase os

questions.text: How do you want success judged for this campaign — completed OS-to-EMI bookings, requests started, outstanding balance moved onto EMI, or some other measure you already track?

Who should this campaign actually reach: customers who have an eligible outstanding balance but have not started converting it (top-of-funnel awareness), or customers who already started an OS-to-EMI request that is sitting pending/incomplete (recovery/completion)? These need different entry points and the platform can only reliably detect the second today.

Do you already have a view on why eligible customers aren't converting — e.g. unaware the option exists, put off by interest/cost, or the process feels like too much effort? This shapes what the messages say, not who they go to.

Should this campaign reach customers who have an eligible outstanding balance but haven't started an OS-to-EMI request yet (top-of-funnel awareness), or customers who already started an OS-to-EMI request that's sitting pending/incomplete (recovery/completion)? Note: the platform can reliably detect the second today via EMI Request status; it has no attribute for 'has an eligible outstanding balance' so the first would need a different, less precise entry point if you choose it.

When you say interest-cost hesitation, which part is it — the interest rate itself, the total interest payable over the tenure, the size of the monthly instalment, or the hit to their available credit limit? This decides what the first message leads with.

The buildable entry (active accounts) cannot exclude customers who already have an EMI Request of any status (Pending, Failed, Expired, Cancelled) because entry can only filter one entity's attributes and there is no cross-entity 'no existing request' condition available. That means some customers who already started a request — the exact group you said you did NOT want to reach — will receive these messages. Do you want to proceed with this broader reach accepted, or hold the campaign until a buildable exclusion exists?

answers.text: No fixed target — success is more EMI Requests reaching Successful. We think interest-cost hesitation is the barrier. Our hunch is balances above 25,000 rupees convert better, and urgency rises near the statement due date.
Target customers who are eligible but have never started a conversion request.

facts.statement: No fixed target — success is more EMI Requests reaching Successful. We think interest-cost hesitation is the barrier. Our hunch is balances above 25,000 rupees convert better, and urgency rises near the statement due date.
Target customers who are eligible but have never started a conversion request.

dimensions.name: Success measure (business definition)
dimensions.rationale: The business's own yardstick for 'this is working' is theirs to give; it determines what measurement.md tracks and how the goal is framed, separate from the platform goal event.
dimensions.note: Success is more EMI Requests (Source=OS-to-EMI) reaching New Status=Successful. No fixed numeric target.

dimensions.name: Target population: not-yet-started vs started-but-stalled
dimensions.rationale: These are different people, at different points in the sequence, reachable through different events. It is a fork: it changes entry, audience and the core intervention (awareness vs. completion nudge).
dimensions.note: Confirmed: eligible customers who have never started a conversion request (top-of-funnel awareness), not recovery of stalled requests.

dimensions.name: Perceived barrier to conversion
dimensions.rationale: If the user already suspects why customers don't convert (cost fear, unawareness, friction), that belief should drive message content; it is their hypothesis about cause, not something I can look up.
dimensions.note: User believes interest-cost hesitation is the barrier. Rather than asking which specific reading (rate, total interest, instalment size, limit impact) since the user is unlikely to know precisely, this is carried into the design as two testable framings (affordability vs total-cost transparency) in an experiment. This is the user's own explanation, carried as a hypothesis: it has not been tested and competing explanations may remain.

dimensions.name: Outstanding balance size / amount involved
dimensions.rationale: A customer with a large revolving balance may warrant different urgency or channel than one with a small balance. Could matter, but the platform exposes no balance or amount attribute on Account for OS-to-EMI, so even a strong answer here may not be buildable as targeting — only as message tailoring. Deferring the question until the fork above is settled, since it only matters within whichever audience is chosen.
dimensions.note: Hunch that balances above ₹25,000 convert better. No outstanding-balance or running-balance attribute exists on any entity (confirmed via list_audience_attributes), so this cannot be built into entry or segmentation. Carried as an unproven hypothesis for future measurement only. This is the user's own explanation, carried as a hypothesis: it has not been tested and competing explanations may remain.

dimensions.name: Timing relative to statement due date
dimensions.note: Hunch that urgency rises near the statement due date. Account has a Statement Due Date attribute, but no confirmed way to express a per-customer relative/dynamic date trigger (e.g. 'N days before each customer's own due date') was found. Carried as a hypothesis; the journey uses fixed-interval spacing instead of due-date-anchored timing. This is the user's own explanation, carried as a hypothesis: it has not been tested and competing explanations may remain.

dimensions.name: Entry/audience buildability gap (eligible, never-started)
dimensions.note: No attribute on Customer or Account represents an outstanding balance or OS-to-EMI eligibility, and entry audience can only filter one entity's attributes — it cannot also exclude customers who already have an EMI Request (any status) on a different entity. The buildable audience is therefore broader than the intended one. Raised as a strategic-ambiguity open item, not quietly absorbed.

successCriteria: More EMI Requests with Source=OS-to-EMI reaching New Status=Successful; no fixed numeric target set by the business.

questionResolutions.why: Interest-cost hesitation is a broad cause (APR vs total interest vs instalment size vs limit impact) that the user cannot reliably introspect — asking again risks another non-answer. Instead of guessing one reading, the journey tests two competing framings against each other (affordability vs cost-transparency) as a controlled A/B, which resolves it with evidence rather than a further question.
